forecasts.claim: If the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed beyond roughly three weeks, global recession begins to take hold and countries around the world intervene to stop the closure.

state_history.reason: First-party source contains an explicit three-week threshold connecting sustained Hormuz closure with emerging global recession and international intervention.

Independent events show severe disruption persisted well beyond three weeks and included a temporary April 17 reopening followed by near-standstill traffic, but the forecast cannot yet be resolved until 'closed', the interval start, 'global recession begins to take hold', and 'countries put a stop to it' are operationalized from the original source context and independent macroeconomic evidence.

forecasts.calibration_notes: The March 21 base-window boundary is provisional and derived from the independently reported February 28 start of the war/de facto closure plus three weeks. It is not treated as Randolph's verified chosen anchor until the full original context is preserved. The forecast remains unresolved rather than scored right/wrong.

limitations: The first-party source currently preserves a publication date but not a verified clock time.
The operational meaning of 'closed' is unresolved and must be tested against transit-volume evidence rather than treated as a binary label.
The three-week clock anchor is provisional pending full-context verification from the source object.
No macroeconomic recession threshold has yet been selected; doing so before identifying Randolph's intended metric would import an assumption.
The April 17 temporary reopening may be relevant to the intervention portion of the claim, but no causal attribution to Randolph's predicted mechanism is made here.
No aggregate credibility finding is authorized from this single forecast record.
